meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich. You cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lincoln. These maxims come from Rev. William J. H. Boetcker's 1916 leaflet The Ten Cannots, misattributed via a 1942 pamphlet.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — actually William J. H. Boetcker
answer.sourceLine: These are two of the maxims in Rev. William J. H. Boetcker’s leaflet The Ten Cannots (1916). Lincoln scholars find no such wording anywhere in Lincoln’s writings or speeches; the confusion traces to a 1942 leaflet titled “Lincoln on Limitations” ↗ that printed genuine Lincoln quotations on one side and Boetcker’s maxims on the other.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
You cannot bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift.
You cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong.
You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich.
You cannot help little men by tearing down big men.
You cannot lift the wage earner by pulling down the wage payer…
trail: Fact-checkers rate the Lincoln attribution False — the lines are Boetcker’s, not Lincoln’s ↗.
Abraham Lincoln Online catalogs this among the “Non-Lincoln ‘You Cannot’ Quotation ↗” items, crediting Rev. William J. H. Boetcker.
Boetcker’s biography confirms he authored The Ten Cannots in 1916 ↗, later confused with Lincoln via a 1942 leaflet.
source.excerptNote: The two quoted lines are drawn from Boetcker’s list of ten “you cannot” maxims; wording varies slightly across reprints.

sourceLink.text: Abraham Lincoln Online: Non-Lincoln "You Cannot" Quotation

source.rightsNote: The maxims were first published in Boetcker’s 1916 leaflet, well before 1931, placing the text in the U.S. public domain. (The attribution to Lincoln is false regardless of copyright status.)

author.name: William J. H. Boetcker
author.heading: Who was William J. H. Boetcker?
author.bio: William John Henry Boetcker (1873–1962) was a German-born American Presbyterian minister who became a popular public speaker on industrial relations, thrift, and personal responsibility in the early twentieth century. He is best remembered for a 1916 leaflet of aphorisms usually called The Ten Cannots, a set of pro-enterprise maxims that would later be widely — and wrongly — pinned on Abraham Lincoln.

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Abraham Lincoln. Actually from Rev. William J. H. Boetcker, "The Ten Cannots" (1916).

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: For decades these maxims have circulated under Abraham Lincoln’s name, cited by presidents and pundits alike. They are not his.

items.why: The lines appear in none of Lincoln’s documented speeches, letters, or writings, and scholars note they lack his style. Abraham Lincoln Online lists them among non-Lincoln ‘You Cannot’ quotations ↗, and PolitiFact rates the attribution False ↗. President Ronald Reagan repeated the error at the 1992 Republican convention.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Rev. William J. H. Boetcker, who published these lines in his 1916 leaflet The Ten Cannots ↗; a 1942 “Lincoln on Limitations” leaflet that placed real Lincoln quotes beside Boetcker’s maxims seeded the confusion.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The “Ten Cannots” became a staple of American political rhetoric precisely because Lincoln’s name gave a set of turn-of-the-century pro-enterprise slogans the weight of the Great Emancipator. In 1942 the Committee for Constitutional Government, a lobby backed by publisher Frank Gannett, distributed hundreds of thousands of a leaflet titled “Lincoln on Limitations” — genuine Lincoln on one face, Boetcker’s maxims on the other — and careless readers merged the two.
The error has since been repeated at the highest levels, most famously by Ronald Reagan at the 1992 Republican National Convention, cementing a misattribution that fact-checkers still correct today.
context.pull: Lincoln’s name gave a minister’s slogans the authority of the Great Emancipator.
